whyItExists.problem: Not every change in your working folder should go into the next commit. You might fix two unrelated bugs — they deserve separate commits with separate messages.
whyItExists.solution: Git has a two-step save: first you stage changes (git add) to select exactly what goes into the next commit, then you commit (git commit) to permanently save that snapshot with a message.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time you reach a logical checkpoint — a working feature, a bug fix, a refactor. Commit often, with clear messages.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't commit broken code to a shared branch. Don't commit secrets (.env files, API keys, passwords).

explainModes.beginner: git add picks which changes to include in your next save. git commit does the actual saving with a message describing what you did. Think of add as putting things in a box, and commit as sealing the box and labelling it.
explainModes.simple: git add file.html — stages one file. git add . — stages everything. git commit -m 'message' — saves staged changes as a commit. git add -p — interactive, choose which lines to stage (advanced but very useful).
explainModes.standard: The three-tree model: working tree (your files), index/staging area (what will go into the next commit), HEAD (last commit). git add moves changes from working tree to index. git commit creates a new commit from the index and advances HEAD. git diff shows working-tree vs index. git diff --staged shows index vs HEAD.
explainModes.technical: git add stages file content (blobs) and records them in the index. git commit creates a tree object from the index, then a commit object pointing to that tree and the parent commit. The commit hash is a SHA-1 of the commit's content — deterministic and tamper-evident. git commit --amend replaces the last commit (rewrites history — safe only if not yet pushed).
explainModes.deepDive: The index (staging area) lives in .git/index — a binary file mapping filenames to blob hashes. git add -N (intent-to-add) stages a file with empty content, making it visible in git diff. Sparse checkout (git sparse-checkout) lets you partially check out a monorepo, only materialising the files you need. git commit -S signs commits with a GPG/SSH key — required by some teams for verified authorship.

content.text: Git has three zones: your working files, the staging area (index), and the committed history. git add moves changes to the staging area. git commit saves the staging area as a permanent snapshot.

content.code:
# See which files have changed
git status

# Stage specific file
git add index.html

# Stage all changes in current directory
git add .

# Stage part of a file interactively (pick specific lines)
git add -p index.html

# Commit with a message
git commit -m "Add navigation menu to homepage"

# Stage and commit tracked files in one step (skips untracked files)
git commit -am "Fix typo in footer"

content.text: A commit message should complete the sentence: 'If applied, this commit will...' Use the imperative mood. Keep the first line under 72 characters. Reference issue numbers when relevant.

content.code:
# ✅ Good commit messages
git commit -m "Add dark mode toggle to settings page"
git commit -m "Fix login redirect loop on mobile Safari"
git commit -m "Remove deprecated getUserInfo() function"
git commit -m "Bump React from 18.2 to 18.3"

# ❌ Bad commit messages
git commit -m "fix"
git commit -m "changes"
git commit -m "WIP"
git commit -m "asdfgh"

# Multi-line commit message (opens your editor)
git commit
# First line: short summary (under 72 chars)
# Blank line
# Body: explain WHY this change was made, not what

# Unstage a file (keep the change in working tree)
git restore --staged index.html

# Discard changes in working tree (WARNING: unrecoverable!)
git restore index.html

# Amend the last commit message (before pushing)
git commit --amend -m "Better message"

# Amend to add a forgotten file (before pushing)
git add forgotten.js
git commit --amend --no-edit

content.text: Never commit .env files, API keys, passwords, or secrets. Add them to .gitignore immediately. If you accidentally commit a secret, treat it as compromised and rotate it — git history is permanent.

questions.question: What does git add . do?
options: Stages all changed files in the current directory for the next commit
questions.explanation: git add . stages all new and modified files in the current directory (and subdirectories). It does NOT commit — that's a separate step with git commit.

questions.question: Why does Git have a staging area instead of committing directly?
options: It's a legacy from old Git versions
To let you choose exactly which changes go into each commit
To make Git slower and more careful
questions.explanation: The staging area lets you craft precise commits. You might change 5 files but only want to commit 2 of them together. git add -p even lets you stage specific lines within a file.

faq.a: node_modules/, .env files, build output (dist/, build/), OS files (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db), editor files (.vscode/, .idea/), compiled binaries. GitHub provides starter .gitignore templates for every language at github.com/github/gitignore.

faq.q: Can I unstage something after git add?
faq.a: Yes. git restore --staged <file> removes a file from the staging area without touching your working copy. The change stays in your working tree — it just won't be in the next commit.
